name: Fatima Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run six injection moulding machines that make food tubs and lids at Brightform. I check each first tub for flash, the thin extra plastic left when a mould does not seal. I have a vocational certificate and know the line well; my pay is about normal for an operator.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do you handle new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Daniel runs a supermarket depot shift, and our school-age children Mina and Yusuf share the mortgage bills with us in their own way. We have about two months saved and some other factories nearby. I have never used AI tools; I learn a new panel slowly and prefer a person beside the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the moulding crew the grand AI promises came to very little. A lid still needs checking for a thin plastic lip before it goes into a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My six injection machines would probably keep running as they do now. Daniel’s depot shift and my usual factory wage cover the mortgage, and our two months of savings make a small problem manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the rotating day and night shifts and check the first tubs after every mould change. From each full wage month I would pay a little extra on our car loan, then build the reserve toward three months once the loan is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about work in this picture. Nights still tire me, but an ordinary month is something I know how to manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which machine gives you trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Machine three runs hot and machine five sticks on the left. I can hear the change before the tubs start showing flash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you tried AI at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. Mina has used it for school answers, and I make her write out what she actually understood.

say: I would say the **AI promises** came to little on our moulding line.
I would still check each **first tub** for plastic flash.
think: My **six machines** keep making food tubs and lids.
Two **steady wages** and about two months saved can cover an ordinary setback.
do: Keep **rotating factory shifts** and inspect tubs after mould changes.
Pay extra **car-loan principal** from full-month wages.
Build **cash reserve** after the car loan is cleared.
feel: **Calm** about work, though night shifts remain tiring.
S0.quote: My six injection machines would probably keep running as they do now.
fieldNote: Fatima knows **specific machine faults** and expects ordinary shifts under the plateau.
Her debt payments use **new wage surplus**, with reserve building only after the car loan is cleared.

steps.text: Keep rotating shifts and inspect first tubs after mould changes
Pay extra car-loan principal from full-month wage surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that software may change orders and rotas first, while new arms take longer to prove safe on the moulds. I would ask management to post the paid hours clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two pick-and-place arms already stack tubs on part of our line. If the other machines get them and fewer people cover a shift, I could lose paid hours; Daniel’s depot wage alone will not cover our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts and check the next two rosters against my payslips. If my hours are actually reduced, we would stop the weekly takeaway and I would look at posted nearby operator jobs only where pay covers the mortgage; I would ask about paid, supervised arm instruction without pretending a place was offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious on the drive in. I trust my eyes on a tub more than a promise about future staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a computer course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools and do not want an unpaid evening course after a night shift. I would consider safe practical instruction if the factory actually offers paid time and a qualified setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far could you search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are some other factories within a bus trip. I would need a posted vacancy and a wage close to mine before I could move.

say: I would demand **posted paid hours** before a new rota starts.
I would separate **ordering software** from later physical arms.
think: More arms could mean **fewer paid shifts** for me.
Daniel’s **depot pay** cannot carry our mortgage by itself.
do: Keep **current shifts** and compare two rosters with payslips.
Stop **weekly takeaways** after an actual hours cut.
Search **posted nearby operator roles** only at bill-covering pay after a cut.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible cut to her own paid hours.
S1.quote: I trust my eyes on a tub more than a promise about future staffing.
fieldNote: Her **existing pick-and-place arms** make gradual staff reductions credible.
She only **asks about instruction**; later job searching depends on real lost hours, local postings and adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep moulding shifts and compare next two rosters with payslips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell other parents that thinking AGI arrives by 2028, but capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. Brightform tubs and Daniel’s depot pallets could both be handled by machines when those robots work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my machine hours and Daniel’s warehouse hours to disappear around 2031. Our two months saved will not keep a mortgage and two children going through two lost wages; I already wake at night thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the summer trip and streaming now and ask both employers for written staffing dates. If either wage ends, I would apply for posted reachable work only if the pay and hours cover our bills; if no such role appears, I would ask my sister about temporary childcare and the lender about a payment plan before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the prospect of losing both incomes. Having calls to make does not mean someone will offer a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the second car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if we still had a way for both adults to reach paid work. I would check the bus times first, because selling it blindly could cost us a wage sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you learn the robot controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a paid guarded practice place exists. I have never used AI tools, and watching a demonstration would not make me a trained operator.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I would ask both **employers for dates** before rumours spread.
think: I expect **both wages** to fall when capable robots arrive.
Our **two-month reserve** cannot carry two children and a mortgage through two lost wages.
do: Cancel **trip and streaming** and request staffing dates now.
Apply after **lost wages** only for posted reachable bill-covering work.
Ask **family and lender** about temporary help if no adequate role appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major household wage loss and broken sleep.
S2.quote: I would be alarmed by the prospect of losing both incomes.
fieldNote: She anticipates **dual-earner exposure** when physical robots reach the plant and depot.
Her job and support paths retain **real conditions**; a robot-course question is not enrolment.

steps.text: Cancel summer trip and streaming and request written staffing dates
Apply after wage loss for posted reachable bill-covering work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the parent group that thinking AGI around 2031 comes before capable robots around 2034. Five years is enough for the factory to say who will train on paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still need the mortgage wage, even if the children are older. I know I can waste warning time by hoping it goes away, so Daniel and I would put dates on the kitchen calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay fresh surplus wages against the car loan, then save the freed monthly payment after it is cleared. If Brightform offers a funded, paid-time food-safety qualification with a real place, and a posted nearby quality-check job pays our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; if no place opens, I would check local operator postings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but the calendar gives me something to do on Monday. I will not buy a course for a vacancy that is only a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why quality checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already spot a thin lip on a tub before a whole box is wrong. I would still need actual instruction in the quality records and a posted role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son about engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf can study engineering if he wants. I would ask him to speak to working engineers as well, rather than make his choice from my factory fear.

say: I would ask for **paid training dates** before 2034 robots arrive.
I would tell parents **thinking AI** and physical machines have different dates.
think: The **mortgage wage** still matters each month when I reach forty-eight.
A **kitchen calendar** may stop me spending five years in denial.
do: Pay extra **car-loan principal** then save the freed payment from wages.
Enrol in **funded paid-time food-safety training** only with an offered place and adequate posted role.
Apply after **qualification** for that posted nearby quality-check job.
feel: **Anxious**, with a calendar and conditional path.
S3.quote: I will not buy a course for a vacancy that is only a rumour.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to change** softens for a specific practical qualification tied to paid work.
Both enrolment and later **application** require funded paid time, an actual course place and an adequate local posting.

steps.text: Pay extra car principal then save freed wage payment
Enrol if funded paid food-safety place and adequate posted job exist
Apply after qualification for posted bill-covering quality-check job
Check local operator postings if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 and capable factory robots around 2039 give families a decade to plan. Brightform should publish a real staffing schedule, not make us read a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots might handle tubs. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is cleared or Daniel’s depot still pays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep running the moulding machines and put new spare wages against the car loan and then the mortgage. In the first year after 2036, if I am still employed, I would check real rosters; if my hours then fall, I would apply only for posted reachable work paying our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible later cut but less frightened than in the fast picture. Ten years does not pay the mortgage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a care course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the college for the fee and timetable around year five. I would enrol only if a funded paid-time place is actually offered and a posted local care job has suitable hours and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your sign to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written roster cutting my paid shifts is a sign. Machine noise or a manager looking away is not enough for a house decision.

say: I would ask Brightform for a **written staffing schedule**.
I would separate **2036 systems** from 2039 hands-on robots.
think: Our **mortgage and depot wage** are unknown thirteen years ahead.
A distant calendar does not guarantee **paid shifts** at fifty-six.
do: Keep **current moulding shifts** and pay extra debt from new wage surplus.
Check **post-2036 rosters** only if still employed.
Apply after **actual later cuts** only to posted reachable bill-covering work.
feel: **Anxious** about later hours, with more time to prepare.
S4.quote: Ten years does not pay the mortgage by itself.
fieldNote: Her **2026 work** is current; the 2036 roster check requires her still to have the factory job.
The care-course discussion is a **fee enquiry**, while any eventual enrolment requires an offered funded place and adequate job.

steps.text: Keep current moulding shifts and pay extra debt from new wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut both my factory wage and Daniel’s depot wage. Written staffing dates, an offered paid safe training place and real reachable jobs at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the night shift. A machine can work through the night, but my children need a wage from whichever adult is awake.

headlineQuote: A machine can work through the night, but my children need a wage from whichever adult is awake.
portrait: **Fatima**, 43, is an experienced injection-moulding operator with a vocational certificate and detailed knowledge of her six machines.
Her **depot-worker partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, typical pay and roughly two months saved give her some room but no long bridge.
She has **never used AI**, prefers familiar routines and seeks practical paid instruction only when an actual place and role exist.
Rapid robots threaten **both household wages**; five years lets her set dates for debt payment and conditional training.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could cut her factory hours and Daniel’s depot shifts before their two-month reserve grows.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering roles would make the options real.
